strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: efficient fine-grained perception in MLLMs without external RoI annotations or full-model fine-tuning.

Method is well motivated and relatively simple: pseudo-label generation denoises internal attention maps via sink-token removal and selective label assignment, then trains a lightweight RPN on frozen MLLM features.
The RPN enables a single partial forward pass for RoI prediction, decoupling localization from slow autoregressive decoding and avoiding multi-pass operations.
Strong empirical gains across multiple base models (LLaVA-1.5-7B/13B, DeepSeek-VL-1.3B/7B) and benchmarks, e.g. V* +17.2, TextVQA +12.6, DocVQA +12.4 for LLaVA-7B.
Good ablation studies on pseudo-label components, sink-token removal, label assignment, backbone depth, RPN depth, smoothing strategy, and data efficiency.
Demonstrates data efficiency and practical training cost: competitive throughput relative to ViCrop and training completes in a few hours on the full 152K subset.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported with training hyperparameters, algorithm details, and prompt templates, though some details remain missing.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the work combines existing ideas (attention-based RoI, self-distillation, lightweight RPN) without a fundamentally new mechanism; the theoretical appendix is post-hoc and relies on simplified noise assumptions.

No direct quantitative evaluation of RoI localization quality (e.g., IoU, recall, precision against ground-truth boxes). Downstream QA gains could partly reflect cropping/upscaling effects rather than precise localization.

The abstract and introduction imply main results are obtained with only 10K QA pairs, but the main tables appear to use the full 152K training set; the 10K setting achieves about +7.2 average improvement, not >10 average, so the claim is misleading.

Several reproducibility details are missing: the norm threshold τ_norm, Gaussian filter σ, binary threshold τ, and exact layer-selection protocol are not fully specified; these choices may be benchmark-tuned.

Baseline positioning and comparison are incomplete: S2 is described as a full-tuning method, which may be inaccurate, and there is no comparison to other recent RoI/high-resolution methods or LoRA/full fine-tuning baselines.

Efficiency evaluation is relative and incomplete: no absolute latency, memory, token-count, batch-size, or stage-wise breakdown is reported; two-stage inference still reduces throughput to 0.62× the baseline, so claims of efficiency should be more nuanced.
Main results lack variance/statistical significance reporting, and multi-turn inference behavior is not fully specified; some design choices may overfit to the selected benchmarks.

strengths: Targets an important and timely problem: efficient fine-grained perception via region-of-interest processing in MLLMs.
Annotation-free pseudo-label generation from internal attention avoids costly RoI annotations and is a practical direction.

The lightweight RPN design enables RoI prediction with a single partial forward pass, decoupled from auto-regressive decoding; it is faster than ViCrop in the RoI stage and has better throughput than ViCrop overall.
Reports substantial empirical gains on multiple benchmarks (DocVQA, TextVQA, V-Star, OCRBench) and across LLaVA-1.5 and DeepSeek-VL, including data-efficiency claims with 10K training samples.
Extensive ablation studies cover pseudo-label components, backbone/RPN depth, training data size, smoothing, and upscaling strategies.
Clear algorithm and implementation details (hyperparameters, layer choices, prompts) support reproducibility to some extent.
LLM usage is disclosed in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: attention-based RoI, sink-token removal, thresholded pseudo-labels, and RPN initialization from MLLM layers are largely adapted from prior work; the 'self-distillation' framing is loose and the contribution is mainly an engineering combination.

Evaluation fairness is questionable: baseline LLaVA-1.5 numbers (e.g., TextVQA 46.1) are much lower than commonly reported, inflating gains; ViCrop's cropping strategy is disabled on V-Star, crippling that baseline; the S2 comparison lacks controlled training/compute; DeepSeek-VL is only compared to the baseline, not S2/ViCrop.

Pseudo-label generation depends on several thresholds (tau_norm, tau_fg, tau_bg, smoothing threshold) with little sensitivity analysis; tau_norm is not reported in the main paper, harming reproducibility.

Train-test mismatch: pseudo-labels are derived from response-to-image attention, but inference uses only question tokens to predict the RoI; there is no analysis of failure cases where the question alone cannot recover answer-conditioned attention.

Self-distillation uses the MLLM's own generated responses, including incorrect ones, without filtering or robustness analysis; the counterintuitive claim that self-generated responses outperform ground-truth responses is under-supported.

The efficiency story is nuanced: overall throughput is 0.62x baseline (slower than baseline), and S2 achieves 0.70x throughput with 30.7 average vs SD-RPN's 0.62x with 34.3 average; the method is not Pareto-superior to all baselines.
Main results lack statistical significance tests; error bars appear only in ablations, and large gains are not validated with multiple seeds or confidence intervals.

Reproducibility is limited: the code URL is missing in the manuscript, and several details (exact response generation settings, mask/bbox handling, threshold values) are absent or relegated to the appendix.

The theoretical appendix proves denoising via conditional expectation, but the actual method uses binarized/ignored-label classification; the theory does not directly validate the proposed label assignment strategy.

Positioning and related work are incomplete: several recent high-resolution/RoI MLLM methods are discussed but not compared, and the paper does not establish clear advantages over all relevant baselines.

strengths: Annotation-free and self-distilled framework that avoids external annotations and full-model fine-tuning, making RoI-based fine-grained perception more scalable.
Clear and practical pipeline: attention-map denoising, sink-token removal, selective label assignment, and a lightweight RPN that predicts RoIs in a single partial forward pass.
Strong empirical results across multiple MLLM backbones and benchmarks, with particularly large gains on text-rich and vision-centric tasks such as TextVQA, DocVQA, and V-Star.
Good data efficiency: competitive or superior performance even when trained on only 10K QA pairs, significantly reducing supervision requirements.
Thorough ablation studies on pseudo-label generation, backbone depth, RPN depth, data size, and smoothing strategy, which support the main design choices.
Efficiency-oriented design decouples RoI prediction from autoregressive decoding and compares favorably against ViCrop in throughput while achieving higher accuracy.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method combines existing ideas such as attention-based localization, self-distillation, lightweight RPNs, and crop-based high-resolution processing; the technical contribution is mainly engineering rather than a fundamentally new paradigm.

Baseline comparison is limited to S2 and ViCrop. Several relevant high-resolution or RoI-based MLLM methods (e.g., VILA-HD, LLaVA-UHD, other training-free or training-based RoI selectors) are not compared, and the fairness of comparison to full-tuning S2 is not fully established.

Efficiency claims rely mostly on relative throughput; absolute latency, memory usage, FLOPs, and a detailed breakdown of the two-stage inference cost are missing. The training cost of pseudo-label generation and RPN training is mostly relegated to the appendix.

Pseudo-label quality depends on the MLLM’s own generated responses and internal attention, which may reinforce model biases or noise. The surprising finding that ground-truth responses hurt performance is interesting but not deeply analyzed.

Main results appear to be single-run without variance or confidence intervals; improvements are highly uneven across benchmarks (e.g., ChartQA, InfoVQA, POPE show small gains), which weakens the strength of some claims.

The abstract claims “over 10% absolute accuracy improvement” on unseen benchmarks, but the average gain on the five Document & OCR benchmarks is around 6.4%; this is somewhat overclaimed unless interpreted per benchmark.
Inference design details are underspecified in places, such as how high-resolution visual tokens are inserted for multi-turn conversations and how the method behaves when no clear RoI is predicted.

strengths: Proposes an efficient, annotation-free self-distillation framework that trains a lightweight RPN on frozen MLLM middle-layer features to predict RoIs in a single partial forward pass, avoiding slow autoregressive decoding or multi-pass attention extraction.

Introduces a sensible pseudo-label denoising pipeline: removes sink tokens via feature norms, performs selective high-confidence FG/BG assignment, and ignores ambiguous regions, which is validated by ablations.
Broad and consistent empirical gains across LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, DeepSeek-VL 1.3B/7B, and Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B on multiple OCR/document, vision-centric, hallucination, and high-resolution benchmarks.
Demonstrates good data efficiency: notable improvements even with 10K training samples, and ablations analyze backbone depth, RPN depth, thresholds, smoothing, and upscaling strategy.
Provides efficiency analysis and comparison with external grounding models, showing the RPN prediction step is much faster than Grounding-DINO and better trade-off than naive resolution scaling.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method largely combines existing ideas of attention-based RoI cropping, self-distillation, and a small RPN, with the main algorithmic contribution being a heuristic pseudo-label denoising pipeline.

Several hyperparameters (e.g., τ_fg, τ_bg, layer selections, R) appear selected using the same test benchmarks used for final evaluation, with no held-out validation protocol; this undermines the reliability of reported gains.

The abstract/claims emphasize training on only ~10K QA pairs, but the main results and several analyses appear to use the full 152K-sample training set, creating an unresolved mismatch between headline claims and experimental setup.

Evaluation settings are sometimes unclear or inconsistent: e.g., TextVQA is claimed to be evaluated without OCR tokens, but appendix comparisons include OCR-token results and different numbers, complicating fair interpretation.

The self-distillation target is generated from the model's own possibly incorrect responses; while the paper argues representational consistency, it does not deeply analyze failure modes or error amplification from self-generated attention.

Important implementation details are lightly specified: multi-turn inference with an RPN trained on response-conditioned attention is not fully described, and the code URL is blank, limiting reproducibility.
Some notation/typographical issues and equation bugs (e.g., duplicate symbols in BCE loss, missing scaling factor/mask details) reduce clarity.

strengths: Addresses an important trade-off in MLLM fine-grained perception: using internal attention for RoI localization while avoiding expensive full-model fine-tuning and slow auto-regressive RoI identification.
Proposes a self-distilled pseudo-label pipeline that removes sink tokens and ignores ambiguous foreground/background regions, enabling annotation-free RPN training.
Reports consistent gains across several MLLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5, DeepSeek-VL, Qwen2.5-VL) and benchmarks, with strong improvements on DocVQA, TextVQA, and V-Star.
Provides useful ablations on pseudo-label components, backbone depth, data efficiency, and thresholds, plus training details and algorithm pseudocode.
Efficiency is improved relative to a training-free cropping baseline (ViCrop) by using a single partial forward pass rather than multi-pass or auto-regressive RoI identification.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method combines existing ideas such as attention-based RoI localization, pseudo-label denoising, self-distillation, and middle-layer RPNs, without a fundamentally new mechanism or theoretical insight.

There is a train/inference mismatch: the RPN is trained to predict response-to-image attention from the full generated response, but at inference it uses only the final user-question token(s). This discrepancy is not analyzed or ablated.

The claim that self-generated responses yield better pseudo-labels than ground-truth responses is counterintuitive and only weakly justified; it may indicate overfitting to model-specific attention artifacts rather than learning robust localization.

The pseudo-label generation ignores potentially wrong low-resolution answers: if the base MLLM answers incorrectly, the response attention may focus on the wrong region, yet the paper does not quantify how often this corrupts supervision.

Evaluation fairness is questionable: SD-RPN uses additional 10K–152K QA samples to train the RPN, while the baselines are not given an equivalent lightweight fine-tuning budget. A controlled comparison against standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning on the same data is missing.

Some headline gains are surprisingly large on relatively small benchmarks (e.g., V-Star), and the paper does not provide oracle RoI or grounding-based upper bounds to contextualize how much of the gain comes from RoI quality versus extra training/tuning.

The efficiency claim is overstated: throughput drops to roughly 0.62× the baseline, and the comparison to ViCrop only shows that it is less slow, not that it is efficient in absolute terms. It also does not fully rule out simply increasing the baseline resolution.

Comparison to recent methods is mixed: on V-Star, DeepEyes achieves 90.1 overall versus SD-RPN's 89.5, yet the paper characterizes SD-RPN as comparable or superior without sufficiently nuanced discussion.

Presentation and reproducibility issues remain: numerous typos, inconsistent numbers across tables (e.g., Table 1 vs. Table 11), confusing layer/weight-sharing descriptions, and a missing/blank code URL.
The theoretical appendix is largely trivial and does not directly justify the specific label-assignment and thresholding choices used in the method.
Failure modes are acknowledged (incomplete activation, localization error, spatial relationship errors) but not addressed, which limits the practical significance of the approach.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical problem in MLLM fine-grained perception: efficiently identifying RoIs without large-scale box annotations or full-model fine-tuning.

The proposed SD-RPN is technically sensible: it distills denoised response-to-image attention into a lightweight RPN attached to frozen middle layers, enabling single-forward RoI prediction without autoregressive decoding.
The pseudo-label generation pipeline is simple but effective, with ablations showing that label assignment and sink-token removal both contribute substantially.

Empirical evaluation is broad and convincing: consistent gains across LLaVA-1.5, DeepSeek-VL, and Qwen2.5-VL on OCR/Document, V-Star, POPE, and HR-Bench, including strong data efficiency with only 10K training samples.

The paper provides useful ablations on backbone depth, RPN depth, training data size, thresholds, and upscaling strategies, as well as efficiency comparisons against ViCrop and external grounding models.
Reproducibility is relatively strong: code is promised, training details and hyperparameters are provided, and the method is integrated into established MLLM families.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than breakthrough: the method combines existing ideas—attention-based RoI selection, self-distillation, and lightweight RPN training—into a practical pipeline, but the individual components are not fundamentally new.

The “annotation-free” framing is slightly overstated: the method still relies on question-answer data and model-generated responses to construct pseudo-labels; it avoids RoI/box annotations, but not all supervision.
Overall inference throughput is still lower than the single-stage baseline (roughly 0.4–0.6×), so the efficiency claim is primarily relative to other two-stage RoI methods rather than absolute.

Some choices are heuristic and model-specific, including selected attention layers, frozen backbone depth, and thresholds; τ_norm is not clearly reported in the main text, and the final best threshold setting (τ_bg=0.05) is introduced late and may not be used in the main results.
On the strongest modern baseline (Qwen2.5-VL), gains are consistent but more modest than on older models, and comparisons to recent RL/tool-based approaches are limited mainly to one benchmark.
